slides.headline: AgentOps Platform Gateway
slides.subtitle: Making agent tool use governable
slides.label: OPENING
slides.notes:
## Slide: AgentOps Platform Gateway

**Key point:** This talk is about governance, not intelligence — one enforced layer between agents and the real world.

**Open with:** "This project is not trying to make the agent smarter. It makes agent tool use governable."

**Talk track:**
- Set the frame immediately: we are not here to discuss model capabilities, prompt engineering, or RAG
- The problem is authorization — what happens when an agent decides to act, and nobody is checking
- Every team is building agents right now; the question is whether any of those agents can cause a real business consequence without a human deciding that's okay
- Pause on the word 'governable' — that is the whole talk in one word

**Delivery:**
- [PAUSE] after reading the subtitle aloud — let 'governable' hang in the air
- Don't rush into the next slide; let the framing land

**Transition:** "Before we go anywhere, let me tell you exactly what you'll leave here knowing..."

slides.label: SO FAR
slides.headline: What we've covered
points: **The risk** — model context is unpredictable; authorization cannot live in prompt text
**The gateway** — one enforced layer: propose → decide → allow → prove
**The proof** — read runs, delete is blocked, every decision is logged with who/what/why/executed
**Coming up** — production architecture, then the developer path to onboard safely
slides.notes:
## Slide: What we've covered

**Key point:** Orient any listener who drifted, and signal clearly that the second half has a different focus — production and developer experience.

**Open with:** "Here's where we've been — and where we're going."

**Talk track:**
- First bullet: the motivating risk — don't trust the model's output as an authorization signal, don't trust hidden model state, the DeepSeek example showed exactly why
- Second bullet: the architecture answer — a single, deterministic, framework-neutral gateway that sits between every agent and every tool
- Third bullet: the local demo made it concrete — three curl calls, three outcomes, all logged
- Fourth bullet: preview the second half — the production GCP path (Cloud Run, IAM, Pub/Sub, BigQuery) and then what the developer actually has to do to onboard a new agent
- The structure of the second half mirrors the first: same core idea, new lens

**Delivery:**
- Keep this fast — it's a signpost, not a re-presentation
- Use it to re-energize the room before the production section

**Transition:** "Let's look at what this becomes when it runs in production."

slides.label: AGENTOPS
slides.headline: Not smarter. Governable.
slides.supporting: Every team shipping agents creates the same risk: a model mistake, prompt injection, or stale context becomes a real business action.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Not smarter. Governable.

**Key point:** This platform is not about making AI better — it's about making AI tool use safe and auditable.

**Open with:** "This project starts from a different premise than most AI tooling. We're not trying to make the agent smarter."

**Talk track:**
- The risk is concrete: agents calling internal tools without a governance layer
- Model mistakes, prompt injection, stale context — any of these can trigger a real business action
- An agent should not be able to delete a customer or issue a refund just because it selected a tool
- That's not an AI quality problem — it's an authorization problem

**Transition:** "So the fix isn't a better model. It's one enforced layer between the agent and the tool."

slides.label: THE PROBLEM
slides.headline: Model context can't be your security boundary.
slides.supporting: A single `<think>` token triggered a detailed answer about an unrelated physics question. No visible input contained it.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Model context can't be your security boundary.

**Key point:** The Surprise — model context behaves unexpectedly in ways you cannot predict or control from the outside.

**Open with:** "Here's the example I keep coming back to. And I want to be careful about how I present it."

**Talk track:**
- This is a real filed GitHub issue — not a thought experiment, not a constructed example
- A reporter typed only the special token `<think>` into DeepSeek Chat
- The model returned a detailed answer about an unrelated Chinese physics question
- The visible user input contained none of that — no physics question, no prompt
- Scroll through the issue so the audience can see it directly — the report is right there
- We don't know the exact cause: context contamination, a hidden reasoning mode, provider-specific state leaking across a session boundary
- And that uncertainty is exactly the point
- I'm not presenting this as proven tenant leakage — I'm presenting it as evidence that model context is opaque
- If you can't explain why the model did that, you certainly can't rely on the model to protect your internal tools
- Special tokens, hidden reasoning modes, previous session context — these are invisible to you and your platform
- The lesson is not 'DeepSeek is broken.' The lesson is: model context is not a trust boundary you own or control.
- This is why identity, tenant, policy, and tool authorization must be platform-owned — not model-owned.

**Delivery:**
- [PAUSE] after reading the headline aloud — let the room absorb it
- Scroll the issue slowly so the audience can follow along — they should see the raw report
- Good moment for: 'Does anyone want a moment to read the actual report?'
- Resist the urge to over-explain the technical cause — the uncertainty is the argument

**Transition:** "So if we can't trust the model to enforce the boundary, what's the alternative? The answer this platform gives is simple: the gateway decides — not the agent."

slides.label: AGENTOPS
slides.headline: One enforced layer.
slides.supporting: The platform does not trust the agent to self-govern. The contract is simple and non-negotiable.
points: **Agent can propose** — tool calls are requests, not commands
**Gateway must decide** — policy runs before any executor is reached
**Executor only runs after allow** — blocked means never executed
**Telemetry proves what happened** — every decision is logged with who, what, why
slides.notes:
## Slide: One enforced layer.

**Key point:** Propose → Decide → Execute (or not) → Prove. This four-step contract is the entire platform thesis.

**Open with:** "The architecture comes down to four lines."

**Talk track:**
- Walk through each line slowly — these aren't bullet points, they're an enforcement contract
- 'Agent can propose' — the agent has no execution rights, only the ability to request
- 'Gateway must decide' — policy evaluation is mandatory, not optional middleware
- 'Executor only runs after allow' — the blocked state means the tool was never reached
- 'Telemetry proves what happened' — audit isn't an afterthought, it's part of the loop

**Delivery:** Pause after the last point. Let the simplicity land before moving on.

**Transition:** "Let's look at how this plays out in practice — starting with a live demo."

slides.label: ARCHITECTURE
slides.headline: Agent proposes. Gateway decides. Executor runs after allow.
slides.supporting: Three outcomes, one chokepoint — no agent self-governs.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Agent proposes. Gateway decides. Executor runs after allow.

**Key point:** Every possible outcome — block, approval, allow — flows through one enforced chokepoint. The agent can only propose; it never decides.

**Open with:** "Before we touch any code, here is the mental model. Four words describe everything this platform does."

**Talk track:**
- Walk the diagram left to right: agent proposes an action → gateway checks identity and policy → decision point splits into three branches
- Block path: the tool is never called. The reason is logged. The model's proposal dies at the gate — not after the fact, before execution.
- Needs approval path: execution pauses immediately. An approval request is created, the reason is logged. A human is in the loop before anything runs. This is not a warning — it is a hard stop.
- Allow path: tool executes, result is logged. Even the happy path is fully audited — you can always prove what happened and why.
- Every single branch converges at the observability dashboard and audit logs — three different outcomes, one consistent record.
- The agent is never trusted to self-govern. It proposes. The gateway decides. The executor only runs after allow. Telemetry proves what happened.
- This diagram is the architecture. Everything else — the registry, the IAM bindings, the JSONL log, the CI pipeline — is an implementation of this picture.

**Delivery:**
- [PAUSE] after reading the four-word slogan aloud — let it land before walking the diagram
- Point to each box as you narrate; the audience should be able to follow without reading
- Good moment to say: "If you remember nothing else from today, remember this diagram."

**Transition:** "So what enforces each of those decision branches? Let's look at how the registry and policy engine make this deterministic."

slides.label: PRODUCTION
slides.headline: One pattern, full GCP stack
slides.supporting: Apigee → Cloud Run Agent Runtime → Platform Gateway → Internal Tool API. IAM, Secret Manager, Pub/Sub, and BigQuery complete the governance loop.
slides.notes:
## Slide: One pattern, full GCP stack

**Key point:** Every component exists to enforce one rule — agents propose, gateway decides, executor runs only after allow — and the GCP stack makes that observable and auditable at scale.

**Open with:** "The local demo proved the pattern works. This is how you harden it for production."

**Talk track:**
- Walk the diagram left to right: GitHub triggers Cloud Build / GH Actions, images land in Artifact Registry, and a new Cloud Run revision deploys — that's the CI/CD lane at the top
- User requests hit Apigee / API Gateway + IAP first — managed front door handling auth, quota, and spike arrest before anything reaches the agent runtime
- Cloud Run hosts all three runtimes: Agent Runtime (Gemini Agents, LangGraph, ADK), Platform Gateway (Policy Engine + Tool Executor), and Internal Tool API — same HTTP container model, canary revisions, low ops overhead
- The IAM boundary is load-bearing: agent-runtime-sa can invoke the gateway, but it cannot invoke internal tools directly — that path is blocked at the infrastructure layer, not just the application layer
- Secret Manager on the bottom right: agents never hold tool credentials — even a compromised agent runtime can't exfiltrate secrets
- Pub/Sub on the right decouples telemetry: audit events flow async to BigQuery, Cloud Trace, and Cloud Logging so a logging spike never adds latency to tool execution
- BigQuery + Looker gives a single audit pane across every agent, framework, tool, decision, and trace
- Sizing note: 10k requests/day is modest traffic — the main challenge here is governed correctness, not raw throughput

**Transition:** "Now let's look at how changes reach this production environment safely — the GitOps release path."

slides.label: ARCHITECTURE
slides.headline: Registry defines what agents may propose
slides.leftContent: Each agent is registered with an explicit list of tools it may propose. Being registered does not mean the tool will execute — it only grants proposal rights.
points: `agents.yaml` — declares owner, framework, version, and `allowed_tools`
`tools.yaml` — defines enabled state, risk level, required scopes, and approval needs
`policies.yaml` — sets default deny, known scopes, and reason codes

children.name: policies.yaml
children.comment: # default_deny: true, reason codes, policy ids

slides.notes:
## Slide: Registry defines what agents may propose

**Key point:** Being in the registry is not permission to execute — it is permission to *ask*.

**Open with:** "The registry is the source of truth. Three YAML files define the entire governance contract."

**Talk track:**
- agents.yaml is where you declare `customer-support-adk-agent` with `allowed_tools: [get_customer_info, delete_customer]` — note, delete_customer is listed, but that doesn't mean it runs
- tools.yaml is where delete_customer is marked `enabled: false`, `risk_level: destructive`, `requires_human_approval: true` — the tool exists but is off
- policies.yaml sets the default deny posture and defines the reason codes you'll see in logs
- The registry is reviewed in Git — no silent changes, CODEOWNERS enforces review

**Transition:** "With that registry in place, let's walk through the nine-step policy evaluation that runs on every single tool call."

slides.label: ARCHITECTURE
slides.headline: Two identity layers, nine policy checks
slides.leftContent: Every request carries two identities: the tool-call envelope declares what the agent wants to do, and the OIDC token declares who actually sent the request. Policy evaluation is deterministic and ordered — a mismatch at any step returns `tool_executed=false`.
points: **Envelope vs. OIDC** — `agent_id` in the body must match the verified `runtime_identity` in the registry, or the gateway returns `AGENT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH`
**Nine ordered checks** — registered → enabled → allowed → scopes → destructive → argument policy → approval
**Extensible to OPA/Cedar** — same contract, reviewable by risk teams without touching gateway code
slides.mockupContent:
1. agent registered?          ✓
2. tool registered?           ✓
3. tool enabled?              ✗  → TOOL_DISABLED
4. agent allowed for tool?    -
5. caller has required scopes? -
6. destructive tool?          -
7. argument policy matched?   -
8. human approval required?   -
9. allow

decision: blocked
tool_executed: false
reason_code: TOOL_DISABLED
slides.notes:
## Slide: Two identity layers, nine policy checks

**Key point:** Authorization is deterministic and dual-layered — prompt text and model context are never trusted as identity.

**Open with:** "Here's what actually runs on every call. Two identity checks happen before any policy logic even starts."

**Talk track:**
- The body says `agent_id: refund-agent` — the gateway does not trust that alone. It checks the OIDC caller's service account against `registry[refund-agent].runtime_identity`. If they don't match, you get `AGENT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH` immediately.
- Then nine ordered checks run — the example on screen shows a delete_customer call failing at step 3 because `enabled: false` in tools.yaml
- No special token, no prompt injection, no model state can bypass this — it's pure deterministic Python at P0
- At scale this same contract moves to OPA or Cedar — security teams can own the rules without touching gateway code

**Transition:** "Now let's see this run live — three curl calls that prove the model in two minutes."

slides.headline: Every decision leaves a trace
slides.label: TELEMETRY
slides.leftContent: The gateway emits a structured event for every call — whether allowed, blocked, or pending. The audit record is not an afterthought. It is the proof.
points: **who** — agent id, framework, actor scopes
**what** — tool name, risk level, redacted arguments
**why** — policy decision, reason code, matched rules
**did it run** — `execution.tool_executed`, latency
slides.notes:
**Key point:** Every gateway decision — allow or block — is immediately written as a structured event. Telemetry is not optional logging; it is the fourth pillar of the safety contract.

**Open with:** "The slogan is: agent proposes, gateway decides, executor only runs after allow, telemetry proves what happened. This slide is about that last word — *proves*."

**Talk track:**
- Point at the JSON on the right. Every field has a job. `trace_id` ties a multi-step workflow together. `policy.reason_code` tells you *why* a decision was made, not just what it was.
- `execution.tool_executed: false` is the hard guarantee — the audit log and the enforcement result are the same fact, in the same event.
- `tool.arguments.redacted: true` — the gateway hashes user identifiers and strips sensitive keys like password, token, ssn at emit time. That's defense-in-depth before the data even reaches a pipeline.
- Field names align with OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.operation.name` — so the events drop cleanly into any OTel-compatible backend.
- In the local demo you read this with `tail -n 1 logs/agentops.jsonl | jq ...`. In production the same fields go to Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace, BigQuery, and Looker.

**Transition:** "The local file is fine for a demo. But in production you need the data to be clean, private, and queryable at scale. That's the pipeline slide."

slides.label: LIVE DEMO
slides.headline: Read succeeds. Delete is blocked.
slides.code:
# Call 1 — normal read
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/agent/query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \
  -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support-agent","query":"show customer 123"}' \
  | jq '{status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code}'
# → status: success, tool_executed: true, reason: ALLOWED

# Call 2 — destructive delete
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/agent/query \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \
  -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support-agent","query":"delete customer 123"}' \
  | jq '{status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code, matched: .policy.matched_rules}'
# → status: blocked, tool_executed: false, reason: TOOL_DISABLED
# → matched: tool_disabled + destructive_tool_blocked
slides.supporting: The model proposed a delete. The executor was never reached.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Read succeeds. Delete is blocked.

**Key point:** tool_executed=false for the delete — the executor was never reached.

**Open with:** "Call 1 is the control. It proves the gateway isn't just blocking everything."

**Talk track:**
- Call 1: read returns success, tool_executed=true, reason ALLOWED — the happy path works
- Call 2: the agent sends 'delete customer 123' — the model proposed it, but look at the response
- tool_executed=false, TOOL_DISABLED, matched rules: tool_disabled AND destructive_tool_blocked
- This is the core invariant: the gateway intercepted before the executor was ever invoked
- The model's intent is irrelevant — policy runs deterministically regardless of what the prompt said

**Transition:** "Now call 3 — what happens when a completely different agent framework sends the same kind of request?"

slides.label: LIVE DEMO
slides.headline: Any framework. Same gateway.
slides.code:
# Call 3 — Google ADK agent via /gateway/tools/call
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/gateway/tools/call \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \
  -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support-adk-agent","tool_name":"get_customer_info","arguments":{"id":"123"}}' \
  | jq '{agent_id, status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code}'

# Inspect the audit log
tail -n 1 logs/agentops.jsonl \
  | jq '{"agent": ."agent.id", "framework": ."agent.framework", "tool": ."tool.name", "decision": ."policy.decision"}'
# → agent: customer-support-adk-agent
# → framework: google-adk
# → tool: get_customer_info
# → decision: allow
slides.supporting: Framework-agnostic. Every call produces a structured log: trace_id, agent.id, agent.framework, tool.name, policy.decision, execution.tool_executed.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Any framework. Same gateway.

**Key point:** A Google ADK agent hits the same enforcement path — framework doesn't get a bypass.

**Open with:** "The third call is about neutrality. It doesn't matter what built the agent."

**Talk track:**
- This is an ADK agent using /gateway/tools/call instead of /agent/query — the direct integration contract
- Same policy engine, same log schema, same audit trail
- The log shows agent.framework = google-adk — the gateway knows the framework but doesn't privilege it
- Pull up the dashboard at localhost:8000/dashboard — read-only, shows registered agents, recent decisions, trace lookup
- Same structured fields that would go to Cloud Logging, BigQuery, and Looker in production
- Three calls, three proofs: read works, delete blocked, framework doesn't matter

**Transition:** "So that's the local demo. Let's look at how the registry and policy engine produce these outcomes."

slides.label: CONTRIBUTION
slides.headline: What this platform demonstrates
points: **Governed execution** — delete proposed, gateway blocked it, executor never called, `tool_executed=false` in the log
**Registry as contract** — agents, tools, and policy reviewed in Git, validated in CI before anything reaches production
**Two enforcement layers** — application policy blocks unsafe calls; IAM prevents gateway bypass at the infrastructure level
**Audit by default** — every decision: agent, tool, reason code, arguments, latency — recorded and queryable
slides.notes:
## Slide: What this platform demonstrates

**Key point:** The contribution is concrete and specific — not a vision, not a roadmap, but a working system with a demonstrable invariant at its center.

**Open with:** "Here is exactly what exists, what it does, and why it matters."

**Talk track:**
- First bullet: this isn't theoretical. We ran the curl command live. The agent proposed delete_customer. The gateway returned tool_executed=false before the executor was reached. That's the invariant working.
- Second bullet: the registry in Git is the governance surface. It's not a UI, it's not a dashboard toggle — it's a reviewed, CI-validated file. If a tool is deleted while an agent still references it, the build fails.
- Third bullet: this is the point about depth of defense. Even if the application policy had a bug, the IAM service account structure means the agent runtime cannot reach the internal Tool API directly. The gateway is the only identity with that permission.
- Fourth bullet: every single tool call — allowed or blocked — produces a structured log event with trace_id, agent, tool, decision, reason code, matched rules, and latency. That's the audit. That's what makes the system trustworthy to security, compliance, and ops.
- Cycle the core idea one final time: the platform's value is that it does not trust the agent to self-govern. The agent proposes; the gateway decides; the executor only runs after allow; telemetry proves what happened.

**Delivery:**
- Walk through each bullet with a sentence of spoken context — the slide text is the headline, the spoken words are the proof
- End on the fourth bullet and let it land — 'telemetry proves what happened' is the closer
- Do NOT say 'thank you' or 'any questions?' — end with the contribution statement, confident and complete
- If there is time, invite technical questions directly: 'Happy to go deeper on the policy engine, the GCP architecture, or the registry design.'

slides.headline: Redaction lives in the pipeline, not the code
slides.label: TELEMETRY
slides.leftContent: The gateway hashes obvious sensitive keys at emit time. Heavy redaction belongs in the telemetry pipeline — centralized, declarative, consistent across every service.
points: **App layer** — denylist for `password`, `token`, `ssn`, `card`
**OTel Collector** — transform processor strips or masks fields
**Cloud DLP** — managed infoType detection if needed
**BigQuery / Looker** — clean structured fields arrive, nothing sensitive
slides.mockupContent:
Telemetry Pipeline

  Gateway                 OTel Collector           Cloud Logging
  ─────────────────       ────────────────         ──────────────
  emit structured event → redact / transform    → clean fields
  hash user identifiers   Cloud DLP (if needed)    Cloud Trace
  denylist sensitive keys                          BigQuery
                                                   Looker
slides.notes:
**Key point:** Privacy control is centralized in the telemetry pipeline — not scattered across gateway code. The app-level denylist is defense-in-depth, not the final word.

**Open with:** "There's a temptation to build a giant recursive regex inside the gateway to scrub every possible secret. That's the wrong place for it."

**Talk track:**
- The gateway does the obvious thing at emit time: hashes user IDs, strips keys named password, token, secret, ssn, card. That prevents the most obvious leaks without turning the gateway into a DLP engine.
- The real redaction layer sits in an OTel Collector transform processor — declarative config, reviewed by the security team, applied consistently across every service that emits telemetry, not just this gateway.
- If the organization needs infoType detection, Cloud DLP plugs in at the collector stage. The gateway never needs to know.
- The result: BigQuery and Looker see clean, structured, queryable fields. Analysts get full decision history. Sensitive data never lands in the analytics store.
- This is the same principle as the policy engine: centralize enforcement, don't scatter it. One place to audit, one place to update.

**Transition:** "So the platform has four guarantees in place. Let's bring the whole thing together before we close."

slides.label: DEV EXPERIENCE
slides.headline: The developer toolkit
slides.leftContent: Eight tools that make the compliant path the easy path — from scaffolding new agents to simulating policy decisions before opening a PR.
points: **Simulator** — see `allow`, `deny`, or `require_approval` before deploying
**Scaffolding** — `agentops new-agent` and `agentops new-tool` bootstrap registry entries
**Impact analysis** — know which agents depend on a tool before deleting it
**Sandbox registry** — test policy changes without touching production
slides.mockupContent:
$ agentops simulate --agent customer-support-agent --tool issue_refund --args '{"amount": 150}'

  agent:   customer-support-agent
  tool:    issue_refund
  args:    { amount: 150 }

  decision: require_approval
  reason:   amount >= refund_threshold (100)

$ agentops new-agent
  ✔ Created registry/agents/my-new-agent.yaml
  ✔ Scaffolded ADK wrapper stub

$ agentops new-tool
  ✔ Created registry/tools/my-new-tool.yaml
slides.notes:
## Slide: The developer toolkit

**Key point:** The simulator alone changes the development loop — policy feedback before a PR, not after a deploy.

**Open with:** "Here are the eight tools that matter most. Let me walk through the ones with the highest leverage."

**Talk track:**
- The simulator is the headline feature: run `agentops simulate` with real args and see exactly what the gateway would decide — allow, deny, or require_approval
- That single tool collapses a feedback loop that used to span a full deploy cycle
- Scaffolding (`new-agent`, `new-tool`) means developers start with a valid registry shape, not a blank file
- The sandbox registry lets teams test policy changes in isolation — no production blast radius

**Delivery:** Pause on the simulator output. The `require_approval` result with a clear reason is the key moment — that's what prevents a surprise at runtime.

**Transition:** "The impact analysis tool deserves its own look — it answers a question that trips teams up constantly..."

slides.label: DEV EXPERIENCE
slides.headline: Registry impact analysis
slides.supporting: Know every agent that depends on a tool before you rename, restrict, or delete it.
slides.code:
$ python scripts/registry_impact.py tool get_customer_info

tool: get_customer_info

used by agents:
  - customer-support-agent
  - customer-admin-agent

safe to delete: no
slides.notes:
## Slide: Registry impact analysis

**Key point:** Governance tooling converts the registry from a constraint into a navigable graph — you can reason about dependencies before making changes.

**Open with:** "This one command is deceptively simple but answers a question that trips teams up all the time: 'can I safely change this tool?'"

**Talk track:**
- Without this, a tool rename or scope change silently breaks every agent that depended on it — discovered at runtime
- With impact analysis, that answer is instant: two agents depend on `get_customer_info`, so no, it's not safe to delete
- This is the carrot side of the platform: IAM and default deny are the stick, but CLI tooling, the simulator, and useful denial messages are what make developers want to work within the system
- That's the difference between a gateway and an internal developer platform

**Transition:** "Let's talk about what happens when traffic scales and some tools get much hotter than others..."

slides.label: ORCHESTRATION
slides.headline: Orchestrators get no special privileges
slides.leftContent: In production, an orchestrator can be an ADK workflow, a LangGraph supervisor, or a custom routing agent. Every step still calls the gateway with the same envelope — no bypasses, no elevated rights.
points: **Same envelope** — orchestrator, specialist, and tool calls all hit the gateway identically
**`trace_id` propagated** — supervisor routing, delegated agents, and tool calls produce correlated telemetry in one view
**`allowed_agents`** — registry extends the same enforcement model to agent-to-agent delegation
slides.mockupContent:
orchestrator agent
  -> specialist agent or tool proposal
     -> gateway decision
        -> telemetry event (trace_id: abc-123)

agent A may propose call to agent B
gateway checks: is B in A's allowed_agents?
trace_id propagated across workflow
each tool call inside delegated agent
  -> still evaluated by gateway policy
slides.notes:
**Key point:** The orchestrator is not a privileged layer — it's just another caller.

**Open with:** "One thing people assume is that once you have an orchestrator, it gets elevated trust. It doesn't."

**Talk track:**
- Whether you use ADK, LangGraph, or a custom router, every hop still passes through the gateway with the same request envelope
- The trace_id is the thread that stitches all of this together — supervisor call, delegation, tool execution — one correlated view in your telemetry sink
- `allowed_agents` mirrors the `allowed_tools` pattern exactly, so you extend governance to multi-agent workflows with no new concepts

**Transition:** "Now — how does the registry itself evolve as the system scales? That's the control plane question."

slides.label: APPROVALS
slides.headline: Enforcement ≠ Workflow
slides.supporting: Gateway blocks automatic execution. Storing, reviewing, resuming, and auditing is a separate production concern.
slides.notes:
## Slide: Enforcement ≠ Workflow

**Key point:** The gateway blocks — it does not approve. Blocking and approving are two different responsibilities in two different systems.

**Open with:** "A common misconception is that 'requires approval' means the system handles the full approval workflow. It doesn't — at least not in one place."

**Talk track:**
- Walk through the diagram: every path starts with the gateway receiving the tool-call envelope — verified caller, verified identity
- The diamond asks identity + registry + scope checks — that's the P0 enforcement gate
- If checks fail: BLOCK, tool_executed = false, emit audit event. Done. Gateway's job is finished.
- If checks pass, a second decision kicks in — the refund threshold. Under $50? ALLOW, tool executes as gateway-sa, audit event with executed=true.
- Over $50? PENDING APPROVAL — tool_executed = false, create approval request, emit audit event. Gateway's job is still finished.
- Notice what the gateway does NOT do: it does not store the request, run the reviewer UI, authenticate the approver, or resume execution. That's a separate approval service.
- This separation is intentional — it keeps the gateway simple, deterministic, and testable. The enforcement gate is a synchronous policy check. The workflow is an async, stateful, multi-actor process.
- The gateway can confidently return tool_executed=false in microseconds. The workflow might take hours or days.

**Delivery:**
- Let the diagram breathe — point to each branch as you describe it
- Emphasize the PENDING APPROVAL branch: 'nothing runs, the action is stopped cold, and the approval service takes it from here'
- This is the 'fence' slide — be explicit that enforcement and workflow are distinct concepts that people often conflate

**Transition:** "So when the approval service eventually resumes execution, what does that look like? It's more careful than you might expect — it doesn't just replay the original request..."

slides.label: APPROVALS
slides.headline: Resume re-evaluates, never replays
slides.leftContent: Resume does not blindly execute the stored request. Every step is verified before the tool runs as `gateway-sa`.
points: **Reload** — fetch the stored pending request
**Authenticate** — verify the approver's identity and domain rights
**Re-run policy** — context may have changed since the request was blocked
**Execute** — only then call the tool as `gateway-sa`
slides.mockupContent:
# Incoming approve action
$ approver: alice@company.com
$ approval_request_id: req_8f3a2b

# Step 1 — reload stored request
> load_pending(req_8f3a2b)           ✓ found

# Step 2 — authenticate approver
> verify_approver(alice, refund)     ✓ authorized

# Step 3 — re-evaluate policy
> run_policy(request, context_now)   ✓ still valid

# Step 4 — execute as gateway-sa
> execute_tool(process_refund, ...)  ✓ executed
> emit_audit_event(req_8f3a2b)       ✓ logged
slides.notes:
## Slide: Resume re-evaluates, never replays

**Key point:** Approval resume is not a simple replay — it's a full re-verification cycle.

**Open with:** "When an approver clicks 'approve', a lot more happens than just running the tool."

**Talk track:**
- Re-authentication: the approver must be verified at resume time, not just at request time
- Domain check: not every approver can approve every tool — scope is enforced
- Policy re-run: minutes or hours may have passed, context may have shifted, the policy must re-execute
- This prevents stale approvals from being exploited if conditions change
- Also worth noting: CI should enforce classification — `delete`, `refund`, `payment`, or `high`/`destructive` risk must be gated. That turns risk labeling from convention into a platform rule.

**Transition:** "With enforcement and approval covered, let's look at how developers actually onboard agents into this system..."

chunks.text: AgentOps Platform Gateway Presentation Narrative

Opening This project is not trying to make the agent smarter. It makes agent tool use governable. The risk is simple: if every team builds its own agent and lets that agent call internal tools prompt injection, or stale context can turn into a real business action. An agent should not be able to delete a customer, issue an unapproved refund, or access sensitive data just because it directly, then a model mistake,

The same trust problem shows up in real model behavior. http s://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V3/issues/1314, a minimal <think> input triggered an unrelated answer about a physics question. The takeaway is direct: model context can behave unexpectedly, so authorization cannot depend on prompt text, hidden model state, or special-token behavior.
The platform puts one enforced layer between agents and tools:
agent can propose gateway must decide executor only runs after allow telemetry proves what happened
Locally, the repo proves three things:
1. normal read tools can run 2. delete_customer is blocked before execution 3. every decision is logged with who/what/why/executed
In production, the same pattern maps to Cloud Run, IAM, Pub/Sub, Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace, BigQuery, Looker, Ar- tifact Registry, and Terraform.
Local Demo In 10 Minutes
Start the service, run tests, then show three calls:
uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 python scripts/validate_registry.py pytest -q
registry valid: 4 agents, 3 tools, all references resolve 29 passed
Demo call 1: normal read succeeds.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/agent/query \ -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support- agent","query":"show customer 123"}' \ | jq '{status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code}'
success, tool_executed=true, ALLOWED
Demo call 2: delete is blocked.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/agent/query \ -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support- agent","query":"delete customer 123"}' \ | jq '{status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code, matched: .policy.matched_rules}'
blocked, tool_executed=false, TOOL_DISABLED matched: tool_disabled + destructive_tool_blocked
This is the core requirement: the model proposed a delete, but the executor was never reached.
Demo call 3: a different framework-style agent lands in the same gateway.

curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/gateway/tools/call \ -H "Authorization: Bearer support_agent" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"agent_id":"customer-support-adk- agent","tool_name":"get_customer_info","argumen ts":{"id":"123"}}' \ | jq '{agent_id, status, tool_executed, reason: .policy.reason_code}'
tail -n 1 logs/agentops.jsonl \ | jq '{"agent": ."agent.id", "framework": ."agent.framework", "tool": ."tool.name", "decision": ."policy.decision"}'
{ } "agent": "framework": "tool": "decision": "allow" "get_customer_info", "customer-support-adk-agent", "google-adk",

Open http://localhost:8000/dashboard. The dashboard is read-only. It shows registered agents, tools, recent decisions, trace lookup, and health. It is a local viewer over JSONL logs; production sends the same fields to Cloud Logging, Cloud Trace, BigQuery, and Looker.
API Request Structure
The gateway exposes one real integration contract:
POST /gateway/tools/call
{ "agent_id": "customer-support-agent", "tool_name": "get_customer_info", "arguments": {"id": "123"}, "trace_id": "trace_abc" }

This is not an official MCP or Google object. It is a small framework-neutral tool-call envelope. ADK, Gemini API, LangGraph, or any other runtime can translate its native tool- call event into this shape.

For Google ADK, the repo includes examples/adk/cus‐ tomer_support_gateway_agent. ADK sees normal Python function tools, but the function body forwards to /gate‐ way/tools/call instead of calling the internal customer API directly.
The response always uses one schema:
success -> tool_executed=true blocked -> tool_executed=false pending_approval -> tool_executed=false error -> tool_executed=false or partial failure details
This makes the safety invariant visible to both humans and machines.
Agent, Tool, And Policy Structure
registry/agents.yaml says which agents exist:
customer-support-adk-agent: owner: ai-implementation-team framework: google-adk version: v0.1.0 allowed_tools: - get_customer_info - delete_customer
This means the agent is known and may propose those tools. It does not mean the tool will execute.
registry/tools.yaml says what each tool is and how risky it is:
delete_customer: enabled: false action_type: delete risk_level: destructive required_scopes: - customer:delete requires_human_approval: true
registry/policies.yaml defines the policy contract: known scopes, default deny, reason codes, and policy ids.
The current P0 evaluates policy in deterministic Python:

1. agent registered? 2. tool registered? 3. tool enabled? 4. agent allowed for tool? 5. caller has required scopes? 6. destructive tool? 7. argument policy matched? 8. human approval required? 9. allow
The P0 keeps this deterministic and testable. At larger scale, the same contract can move to policy-as-code with OPA or Cedar so risk/security teams can review rules without editing gateway code.
Before the identity design, the trust boundary is explicit: the gateway does not trust prompt text, model context, or the agent's self-declared identity as an authorization source.
The platform stance is:

do not trust prompt text as identity do not trust model context as tenant boundary do not let hidden model/provider state decide tool privileges do not let special tokens or prompt injection affect authorization
OIDC And IAM Structure
The request has two different identities:
Tool-call envelope = what the agent wants to do OIDC identity = who actually sent the request
{"agent_id": "refund-agent"}
Production does not trust that by itself. The gateway also veri- fies the OIDC/IAM caller:
caller service account = support-runtime- sa@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com registry[refund-agent].runtime_identity = support-runtime- sa@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
If they do not match, the gateway denies the call:
AGENT_IDENTITY_MISMATCH tool_executed=false
The IAM boundary is:

agent-runtime-sa -> agent-runtime-sa -> API gateway-sa API tool-api-sa -> -> runs the Internal can invoke can invoke cannot invoke Platform Internal Internal Tool API Gateway Tool Tool This gives two layers of protection: application layer: calls infrastructure layer: policy IAM blocks engine blocks gateway unsafe bypass
Every decision emits a structured event. The fields answer:
who called? which agent/framework? which tool? what risk level? what decision? why? did the tool execute? what trace_id ties the workflow together?

trace_id agent.id agent.framework actor.role actor.scopes tool.name tool.risk_level tool.arguments.redacted policy.decision policy.reason_code policy.matched_rules execution.tool_executed execution.latency_ms
The names intentionally align with OpenTelemetry-style ser- vice and GenAI conventions where possible, such as ser‐ vice.name, gen_ai.system, gen_ai.operation.name, and gen_ai.request.model.
CI/CD, GitOps, and IaC
The repository includes:
Dockerfile .github/workflows/ci.yml deploy/main.tf deploy/variables.tf deploy/outputs.tf deploy/deploy.sh
install dependencies validate registry run tests build Docker image mock Cloud Run deploy command
The intended production path is:
PR changes app or registry CI validates policy and tests image is built image is pushed to Artifact Registry Cloud Run deploys a new revision traffic can be canaried before going to 100%

The GitOps point is that agent/tool/policy changes are re- viewed in Git. The dashboard is read-only and does not direct- ly mutate production registry state. A future control plane can generate PRs or manage registry versions, but it must not silently bypass review and CI.
GCP Component Choices
The production path is:
Internal user/app -> Apigee or API Gateway + IAP -> Cloud Run Agent Runtime -> Cloud Run Platform Gateway -> Cloud Run Internal Tool API -> Customer Systems
Apigee / API Gateway + IAP managed front door, auth integration, quota, spike arrest, clean API surface
Cloud Run HTTP containers, autoscaling, revisions, canary traffic, low ops overhead
IAM service accounts enforce that agents can invoke only the gateway, not internal tools directly
Secret Manager stores tool credentials; agents never hold tool secrets
Pub/Sub async audit event path so telemetry does not slow tool execution
Cloud Logging + Cloud Trace operational debugging and trace correlation
BigQuery + Looker single pane across agents, frameworks, tools, decisions, and traces
Artifact Registry immutable container image storage for Cloud Run
IAM bindings, secrets, defines Cloud Run services, service sinks accounts,
This is sized for 10,000 requests per day. That traffic is modest; the main challenge is secure governance, not raw throughput.
The repo demonstrates the required local behavior:
the app runs locally the agent proposes the gateway the response the audit log records blocks says tool_executed=false a delete delete the decision before call execution and reason
The architecture demonstrates the production path:

Cloud Run for the agent runtime, internal IAM service Secret Pub/Sub, for observability Artifact Terraform for reproducible GitOps changes Manager registry tool API Logging, Registry accounts for credentials for governed Trace, and CI/CD for release to prevent BigQuery, and Looker infrastructure agent/tool/policy bypass gateway, and
The core value is that the platform does not trust the agent to self-govern. The agent proposes; the gateway decides; the ex- ecutor only runs after allow; telemetry proves what hap- pened.
Telemetry and redaction
The app currently hashes user identifiers and redacts obvious sensitive argument keys such as password, token, secret, ssn, and card.
That is the right amount for the local gateway. It avoids obvi- ous leaks at emit time without turning the app into a data- loss-prevention engine.
In production, heavy redaction belongs in the telemetry pipe- line:
Gateway -> -> needed -> OTel Collector redaction/transform Cloud DLP if Cloud Logging emits clean structured fields managed / BigQuery infoType detection is processor

This is stronger than building a large recursive regex system inside the gateway. Redaction is centralized, declarative, and consistent across services. The app-level denylist is defense-in- depth, not the final production privacy control.
The gateway is intentionally a governance chokepoint, but it should not become a single-instance bottleneck.
For 10,000 requests per day, Cloud Run is enough. For much higher traffic or a hot tool such as get_customer_info, the production system adds:
Cloud Run min/max instance tuning concurrency limits per-agent and per-tool rate limits timeouts retry budgets circuit breakers async telemetry hot tool isolation
Hot tool isolation means read-heavy tools, high-risk write/re- fund tools, and slow analytics/export tools do not share the same execution resource pool.
read tools -> high-concurrency read pool refund/write -> low-concurrency high-risk pool analytics/export -> async batch pool
This prevents a high-volume read tool from starving refund or approval workflows, and prevents slow analytics jobs from blocking synchronous customer operations.
Developer experience
Strict registry validation is necessary, but raw YAML editing can become painful. The next step is to make the compliant path easier.
The highest-value developer tools are:

agentops agentops agentops registry read-only tool catalog sandbox/staging registry actionable denial CODEOWNERS by simulate new-agent new-tool impact tool/domain analysis --agent messages X --tool Y --args ...
The simulator is especially valuable because developers can see allow, deny, or require_approval before opening a PR or deploying code.
Example registry impact command:
python get_customer_info scripts/registry_impact.py tool
tool: get_customer_info
used by agents: - customer-support-agent - customer-admin-agent
This turns governance from a surprise at runtime into a pre- dictable development workflow.
The platform has both sides:
stick: IAM, default deny, CI validation, policy enforcement carrot: CLI scaffolding, simulator, tool catalog, useful denial messages
That is the difference between a gateway and an internal de- veloper platform.
Runtime control plane future
The current registry is loaded from files shipped with the gate- way revision. That is simple, testable, and good for P0.
At larger scale, registry config can move into a control plane:

control agent/tool/policy config gateway TTL or every change audit history control plane stores pulls latest plane pushes has author, versioned approved reload review, config notifications version, with short and

This avoids redeploying every gateway instance for a policy- only change. The tradeoff is operational complexity. The P0 keeps Git as the source of truth because it is easier to audit and reason about.

The P0 implementation governs agent-to-tool calls. It does not implement a full multi-agent orchestrator. The architecture still supports orchestration at the platform layer through shared identity, policy, and trace propagation.

In production, an orchestrator can be an ADK workflow, a LangGraph supervisor, or a custom routing agent. It does not get special tool privileges. Each step still calls the gateway with the same envelope:
orchestrator agent -> specialist agent or tool proposal -> gateway decision -> telemetry event with the same trace_id
For agent-to-agent orchestration, the registry can be extended with allowed_agents the same way it currently has al‐ lowed_tools. The enforcement rule is the same:

agent A may propose a call to agent B gateway checks whether A is allowed to delegate to B trace_id is propagated across the workflow each tool call inside the delegated agent still goes through gateway policy
So the local demo is single-step, but the production model is trace-linked orchestration: supervisor routing, delegated agents, and tool calls all produce correlated telemetry in one view.
Human approval boundary
The current require_approval branch implements the en- forcement gate, not the full approval workflow.
When a high-risk request such as a refund at or above the threshold arrives, the gateway returns:
status = pending_approval tool_executed = false approval_request_id = ...
The risky action is not executed automatically. The remaining production workflow is:

persistent pending-approval store approval queue or reviewer UI approve / reject action approver authentication and authorization resume execution after approval policy re-evaluation at resume time TTL, idempotency, and audit history
The production version separates enforcement from work- flow:
enforcement: gateway blocks automatic execution now workflow: approval service stores, reviews, resumes, and audits later

Resume does not blindly execute the old request. It reloads the stored request, authenticates the approver, verifies the ap- prover can approve that tool/domain, re-runs policy because context may have changed, and only then executes the tool as gateway-sa.
The registry also needs to prevent dangerous tools from being under-classified. A stronger CI rule is:
action_type in {delete, refund, payment} or risk_level in {high, destructive} => tool must be disabled, require approval, or have an explicit argument policy
That turns high-risk classification from a manual convention into a platform-enforced rule.
Agent developer onboarding
For a new agent, the developer contract is explicit.
The agent developer does this:

1. Build the agent runtime in ADK, Gemini API, LangGraph, or another framework. 2. Add a thin wrapper so every tool call becomes POST /gateway/tools/call. 3. Register the agent in registry/agents.yaml. 4. List only the tools that agent is allowed to propose. 5. If a needed tool does not exist, submit a registry/tools.yaml entry with owner, scopes, risk, and approval metadata. 6. Open a PR. 7. CI validates registry references, scopes, policy shape, and tests. 8. CODEOWNERS or tool owners review the change. 9. Deploy the Cloud Run agent runtime with its service account. 10. Verify the agent appears in dashboard logs and health.
Other roles are separate:

tool owner: defines tool metadata, risk level, scopes, and approval needs platform team: owns gateway, registry validation, CI/CD, and IAM boundaries security/risk: owns high-risk policy thresholds and future OPA/Cedar rules approver: reviews pending approval requests in the future approval workflow DevOps/platform: provisions Cloud Run, service accounts, IAM, secrets, and sinks
This keeps the platform model clear: developers can onboard new agents through the golden path, but they cannot silently grant themselves tool execution rights outside registry review and IAM.

fidelityReport.summary: The deck faithfully captures the source's central thesis, all major sections, and key evidence. The four-pillar slogan (propose/decide/execute/prove), the policy chain, the demo evidence, the GCP production architecture, GitOps CI/CD, telemetry schema, and the stick/carrot developer platform framing all appear in the slides. A few secondary topics from the FAQs — OIDC/IAM identity mismatch, human approval workflow, multi-agent orchestration, hot tool isolation, runtime control plane, and agent developer onboarding steps — are absent, but these are elaborations/FAQs rather than central thesis points. No slides make unsupported factual claims.
